newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan army digs in, refugees run low on food.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan army digs in, refugees run low on food.

text.p: Sri Lankan troops dug in on Tuesday in northern areas captured from Tamil Tiger rebels last week and aid workers appealed for urgent supplies of food for thousands of civilians displaced by the fighting.
"Our troops are consolidating their positions in newly captured areas," army spokesman Brigadier Tissa Jayatunga said.

The army was building bunkers and bringing up fresh troops and supplies in the Omanthai area near Vavuniya, 220 km (135 miles) north of Colombo, before moving deeper into the rebel-held Wanni region, military officials in the north said.

A Christian priest who arrived in Vavuniya from the Wanni told Reuters that civilians displaced by the fighting between the army and Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels were running short of food.
"The food situation is very bad," he said, declining to be identified. "People are appealing for food."
Aid workers in Vavuniya said no food convoys had gone north since the army launched its latest offensive last Tuesday.
"We need to rush 200 truckloads of rice, 200 trucks of flour and 50 truckloads of sugar," said an aid worker.
The military spokesman denied there was a food shortage, saying enough stocks were sent before the offensive began.

Troops backed by tanks, artillery and air cover broke out of their bases in northern Vavuniya and northeastern Welioya last week as part of an operation codenamed "Jaya Sikuru", or "Sure of Victory", in a bid to open a supply route to Jaffna peninsula, 100 km (60 miles) further north.
The Defence Ministry says rebel transmissions intercepted by the troops indicate 181 Tigers had been killed and 316 wounded in the offensive. It said the dead included several leaders.
The rebels have accused the military of killing Tamil civilians and destroying property under the pretext of opening a supply route.
The LTTE said in a statement the government was dramatically exaggerating rebel losses, and that only 60 fighters had been killed while army casualties had been carefully concealed.
Journalists have not been allowed into the battle zone.
According to official figures given by the Defence Ministry, 67 soldiers have been killed and 96 wounded in the offensive. Hospital sources said some 320 soldiers have been wounded.
Military officials said seven soldiers died on Tuesday morning in separate rebel attacks in the north and east.
In fierce fighting last week, troops captured Omanthai, 14 km (nine miles) north of Vavuniya, and Nedunkeni, about 40 km (25 miles) northeast of Vavuniya in the Wanni region.

The LTTE, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in mainly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east, control vast swathes of land in the mostly shrub-covered Wanni, forcing the military to rely on air and sea links to supply Jaffna.

Two army divisions were moving in two separate flanks in what military analysts and diplomats say was an attempt to cut across the LTTE-held areas to ensure that the rebels are spread thinly on the ground and unable to launch a concerted attack on security forces.
But Tamil politicians have appealed to President Chandrika Kumaratunga to stop the offensive.
"It is clear that the strategy of winning peace by military action has failed," Tamil United Liberation Front president M. Sivasithamparam said in a letter to Kumaratunga.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE say the number is higher.
